Q: AttributeError: module 'streamlit' has no attribute '_is_running_with_streamlit'. This attribute used to work properly but now it doesn't work anymore A:

Make sure the name of the file is not the same as the module you are importing – this will make Python think there is a circular dependency; most of the time this error and similar one will be gone by changing the name of the file.py if file name and module name are similar.

Q: Python error log location A:

You should use flask.logging.default_handler instead of logging.StreamHandler(), as the former use request.environ['wsgi.errors']to create stream but latter didn't, refer here for detail.

And for more information about request.environ['wsgi.errors'], see here.

Q: windows registry setting for timeoffset from gmt is not getting updated A:

One usually doesn't program directly against these registry keys. For example, in .Net, we have the TimeZoneInfo class. It uses the same data, but in a much more developer-friendly way.

Regarding your particular question, the ActiveTimeBias key hold the current offset from UTC for the time zone that your server is set to. If your server is in a time zone that follows daylight savings rules, then this will change twice a year. If you manually update your time zone and refresh the registry, you will see it change.

The best advice I can offer is that since the timezone of the server is likely to be unimportant to anyone, you should set it to UTC.

See also: Daylight saving time and time zone best practices

Q: Highlight all cells of identical class in a table A:

To approach this problem, you have to explain your ultimate goal. That is, don't explain the problem in terms of capturing any set of elements. Instead, explain what behavior you want to implement in response to what user action.

In other words, beware of XY Problem.

Q: Does has_secure_password use any form of salting? A:

has_secure_password uses bcrypt-ruby. bcrypt-ruby automatically handles the storage and generation of salts for you. A typical hash from bcrypt-ruby looks like this: $2a$10$4wXszTTd7ass8j5ZLpK/7.ywXXgDh7XPNmzfIWeZC1dMGpFghd92e. This hash is split internally using the following function:

def split_hash(h)
  _, version, cost, mash = h.split('$')
  return version, cost.to_i, h[0, 29].to_str, mash[-31, 31].to_str
end

For the example hash this function yields:

  • version: 2a
  • cost: 10
  • salt: $2a$10$4wXszTTd7ass8j5ZLpK/7.
  • hash: ywXXgDh7XPNmzfIWeZC1dMGpFghd92e

The ==-function of BCrypt::Password extracts the salt and applies it to the passed string:

BCrypt::Password.create('bla') == 'bla' # => true

Q: Optimize, or correct, a code for interpolation and parameter estimation A:

I will lead by saying I doubt that these suggestions will solve your immediate issue (though I think that issue isn't very clearly stated).

The code is... not good. This is a sparse problem and you aren't treating it as such. precompute_paulis reduces to a dual Kronecker product:

import scipy.sparse as sp


def precompute_paulis(n: int) -> tuple[
    list[sp.sparray], list[sp.sparray],
]:
    """Pauli operators (precomputed)"""
    x = []
    z = []
    xpat = sp.coo_array([
        (0,  1),
        (1,  0),
    ])
    zpat = sp.coo_array([
        (1,  0),
        (0, -1),
    ])

    for i in range(n):
        eye = sp.eye_array(1 << (n - i - 1))
        reps = sp.eye_array(1 << i)
        x.append(sp.kron(reps, sp.kron(xpat, eye)))
        z.append(sp.kron(reps, sp.kron(zpat, eye)))

    return x, z

This is likely to change performance but won't improve numerical accuracy (yet).

build_H, after improving Generator usage, reduces to

def build_H(
    n: int, J: float, X: list[sp.sparray], Z: list[sp.sparray], rng: np.random.Generator,
    Delta0: float = 1., delta: float = 1., h: float = 0.3,
) -> sp.sparray:
    """Hamiltonian"""
    Gamma = rng.uniform(low=Delta0 - 0.5*delta, high=Delta0 + 0.5*delta, size=n)
    h_rand = rng.uniform(low=-0.5*h, high=0.5*h, size=n)
    i = np.arange(n)
    j = (i + 1)%n
    Jij = rng.uniform(low=-J, high=J, size=n)
    return sum(
        g*z + h*x + jij*(x @ X[tj])
        for g, h, x, z, jij, tj in zip(Gamma, h_rand, X, Z, Jij, j)
    )

collect_spacings shouldn't be iteratively building a list, and instead should populate a pre-allocated array. More importantly, your eigenvalue problem is on a (3% density) sparse matrix, so don't use eigh. Instead use eigsh and only ask for the first 3*N//4 eigenvalues. I'm sure that you've read the documentation and saw that the eigenvalues are already returned in ascending order, so your call to .sort() was redundant; that remains the case with eigsh due to the default value of return_eigenvectors. Finally, stop resetting your random state in a loop. Make a generator (optionally with a chosen seed) once, and apply it to the simulation. collect_spacings then looks like

def collect_spacings(
    n: int, J: float, X: list[sp.sparray], Z: list[sp.sparray],
    rng: np.random.Generator, n_realizations: int = 500,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Collect unfolded spacings"""
    N = X[0].shape[0]
    lo, hi = N//4, 3*N//4    # middle half of spectrum
    n_diff = N//2 - 1
    all_s = np.empty(n_realizations * n_diff)

    for r in range(n_realizations):
        H = build_H(n, J, X, Z, rng)
        evals = sp.linalg.eigsh(H, k=hi)[0][lo:]
        s_raw = np.diff(evals)
        s = s_raw / s_raw.mean()
        all_s[n_diff*r: n_diff*(r+1)] = s

    return all_s

As to whatever deeper physics/math problem may exist: I'm not convinced that you'd be able to resolve it here. Try cross-posting to Computational Science.

Q: Retrieving multiple data from db and grouping them A:

Well, queries produce a rectangular result set, not a hierarchical one, but something like this would work:

SELECT Color, Make
FROM Cars
ORDER By Color, Make

Then when you display the results you can show the Color only when it changes.
